summary:
Spacumni is an interactive, browser-based 3D globe application that detects and visualizes long-term climate trends in NASA Earth science data. While standard satellite viewers only show static values for a single date, Spacumni analyzes 30 years of NASA MERRA-2 snow depth records (1996–2026) to reveal where snow cover is genuinely increasing, decreasing, or merely fluctuating as random noise.   

To make multi-decade archives fast and accessible, we built an offline Rust pipeline that aggregates raw NetCDF files onto an equal-area Uber H3 hexagonal grid, removes seasonal cycles, and computes trend rates and significance using Sen’s slope and the Mann-Kendall test. The web app loads these pre-computed binary results, letting users explore regional trends, adjust $p$-value thresholds in real time, isolate specific seasons, and inspect 30-year time series without coding or installation.   By removing heavy local processing barriers, Spacumni helps researchers and students quickly spot localized climate shifts—like earlier spring snowmelt—that annual averages often hide.
details:
What It Does & How It Works Spacumni is an interactive 3D globe in the browser that finds long-term climate trends in NASA Earth science data. Instead of showing a static snapshot for a single day, it analyzes 30 years of NASA MERRA-2 snow depth records (1996–2026) to reveal where snow cover is genuinely increasing, decreasing, or just fluctuating randomly.

Under the hood, an offline Rust pipeline aggregates raw NetCDF data onto an equal-area hexagonal grid (Uber H3) and runs non-parametric statistical tests (Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope). The web app then loads these pre-computed binary results so you can spin the globe, adjust the significance ($p$-value) threshold in real time, switch between seasons, and click any region to inspect its 30-year time series.

Benefits & Intended Impact Working with decades of raw satellite grids usually requires coding skills and heavy local processing just to strip out seasonal cycles and find real trends. Spacumni removes that barrier—anyone can open a link and explore regional climate shifts right away, without installing software or writing code. By isolating specific months or seasons (like spring snowmelt), it helps researchers and students spot local changes that annual averages often hide.
